title: Chapter 17. Of the Causes, Generation, and Definition of a Common-wealth
paragraphs: People naturally love liberty and mastery over others. So when we see them impose a restraint on themselves and live in commonwealths, what ultimately causes them to do this — what their design and purpose amount to — is foresight: they can see that this is how they preserve themselves and live more contented lives. In other words, they see it as a way of escaping the miserable condition of war. That war follows necessarily, as has already been shown, from people's natural passions whenever there is no visible power to keep them in awe — no power that, through fear of punishment, ties them to keeping their covenants and observing the laws of nature set out in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters.

The laws of nature — justice, equity, modesty, mercy, and, in sum, doing to others as we would be done to — go against our natural passions if nothing enforces them. Left to themselves, without some power to terrify us into observing them, they are contrary to the passions that drive us toward partiality, pride, revenge, and the like. And covenants without the sword are merely words, with no strength to secure anyone at all. So even granting the laws of nature — which a person keeps only when he is willing to keep them and can do so safely — if no power has been set up, or none great enough for our security, then every man will, and lawfully may, rely on his own strength and cunning as his guard against everyone else. Wherever people have lived in small families, robbing and plundering one another has been a trade — and so far from being considered contrary to the law of nature that the greater the plunder they won, the greater their honor. In this they observed no laws but the laws of honor: that is, to abstain from cruelty, leaving people their lives and their tools for farming. And just as small families did then, so now do cities and kingdoms — which are simply larger families — enlarge their territories for their own security. Under every pretense of danger, fear of invasion, or fear that aid might be given to invaders, they do all they can to subdue or weaken their neighbors, by open force and by secret means, for lack of any other safeguard; and doing so is accounted just, and they are remembered for it in later ages with honor.

Nor does simply joining together in small numbers give people this security. Among small numbers, a small addition of strength on one side or the other is enough to tip the balance decisively and carry the victory — which is exactly what encourages an invasion. The multitude large enough to be relied on for our security is not fixed at any particular number; it is measured against the enemy we fear. It is large enough when the enemy's advantage is not so visible and conspicuous as to determine the outcome of a war, and so not enough to tempt him into attempting one.

However great the multitude may be, if its members act according to their own separate judgments and separate appetites, they can expect no defense or protection from it, either against a common enemy or against injuries from one another. Being at odds in their opinions about how best to use and apply their strength, they do not help but hinder each other, and their mutual opposition reduces their combined strength to nothing. This leaves them easily subdued, not only by a small number who do agree among themselves, but also, when there is no common enemy, prone to making war on one another over their particular interests. For if we could suppose a great multitude of men to agree in observing justice and the other laws of nature without any common power to keep them all in awe, we might just as well suppose all mankind capable of the same thing — in which case there would be neither the need for, nor any such thing as, civil government or commonwealth at all, since there would be peace without anyone being subject to anyone else.

Nor is it enough, for the security that people want to last their whole lives, that they be governed and directed by one judgment only for a limited time, as in a single battle or war. Even if they win a victory through their unanimous effort against a foreign enemy, afterward — once they either have no common enemy, or the one party regards as an enemy someone another party regards as a friend — the difference in their interests will inevitably pull them apart, and they will fall again into war among themselves.

It is true that certain living creatures, such as bees and ants, live sociably with one another — which is why Aristotle counted them among the political creatures — and yet they have no guide beyond their own particular judgments and appetites, nor any speech by which one can tell another what it thinks would serve the common benefit. So someone may well want to know why mankind cannot do the same. To this I answer:

First, that men are continually in competition for honor and standing, which these creatures are not; and consequently, on that ground, envy and hatred arise among men, and finally war — but not among these creatures.

Second, that among these creatures the common good does not differ from the private good; and being by nature inclined to their own private good, they thereby secure the common benefit as well. But man's pleasure lies in comparing himself with other men, so he can enjoy nothing except what stands out above the rest.

Third, that these creatures, not having the use of reason as man does, neither see nor think they see any fault in how their common business is run; whereas among men there are a great many who think themselves wiser and more able to govern the public than the rest, and these strive to reform and change things — one this way, another that way — and so throw it into confusion and civil war.

Fourth, that these creatures, though they can use their voices to some extent to make their desires and other feelings known to one another, lack that art of words by which some men can present what is good in the guise of evil, and what is evil in the guise of good, and can inflate or shrink the apparent size of good and evil — unsettling people and disturbing their peace whenever it suits them.

Fifth, that irrational creatures cannot distinguish between injury and mere damage, and so, as long as they are comfortable, they take no offense at their fellows; whereas man is most troublesome precisely when he is most at ease, for that is when he loves to display his wisdom and to find fault with the actions of those who govern the commonwealth.

Last, that the agreement among these creatures is natural, while agreement among men comes only through covenant, which is artificial. So it is no wonder that something more than covenant is needed to make their agreement steady and lasting — namely a common power, to keep them in awe and to direct their actions toward the common benefit.

The only way to set up such a common power — one able to defend people from foreign invasion and from injuries done by one another, and so to secure them in such a way that, through their own industry and the fruits of the earth, they can feed themselves and live contentedly — is this: to confer all their power and strength upon one man, or upon one assembly of men, who can reduce all their individual wills, by a plurality of voices, to a single will. That is as much as to say: to appoint one man, or one assembly of men, to bear their person, with every one of them owning and acknowledging himself the author of whatever the one who bears their person does, or causes to be done, in matters concerning the common peace and safety — and in that, to submit their wills, each to his will, and their judgments, to his judgment. This is more than consent or agreement; it is a real unity of them all in one and the same person, brought about by a covenant of every man with every man, in such a way as if every man said to every other man, "I authorize and give up my right of governing myself to this man, or to this assembly of men, on this condition, that you give up your right to him and authorize all his actions in the same manner." Once this is done, the multitude so united in one person is called a COMMONWEALTH — in Latin, CIVITAS. This is the generation of that great LEVIATHAN, or rather, to speak more reverently, of that mortal god to whom, under the immortal God, we owe our peace and defense. For by this authority, given to him by every individual man in the commonwealth, he has conferred on him the use of so much power and strength that, through the terror it inspires, he is able to shape the wills of them all toward peace at home and mutual aid against their enemies abroad.

In him consists the essence of the commonwealth, which, to define it, is: "One person, of whose acts a great multitude, by mutual covenants with one another, have made themselves, every one, the author, so that he may use the strength and resources of them all, as he thinks fit, for their peace and common defense."
And the one who bears this person is called SOVEREIGN, and is said to hold sovereign power; and everyone else is his SUBJECT.

Sovereign power can be attained in two ways. One is by natural force — as when a man makes his children submit themselves and their children to his government, since he is able to destroy them if they refuse, or when he subdues his enemies to his will by war, granting them their lives on that condition. The other is when men agree among themselves to submit voluntarily to some man, or assembly of men, trusting to be protected by him against everyone else. This second kind may be called a political commonwealth, or a commonwealth by institution; the first, a commonwealth by acquisition. I will speak first of a commonwealth by institution.
